text.paragraph: Establishing care after recurrent seizures: seizure history, baseline tests, EEG and MRI orders, seizure safety, and gambling-disorder assessment with a safety assessment [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He wants the seizures to stop interrupting his writing and his deadlines. [S]
He wants to stop losing money at roulette and to pay off his debts. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was born in Moscow on 11 November 1821 and died in St. Petersburg on 9 February 1881. [D]
Dostoevsky had epilepsy throughout his literary career; in 1863 he went abroad to seek expert advice from the neurologists Romberg and Trousseau. [D]

Accounts of when his epilepsy began and was diagnosed differ. One account places seizures in his student years (1838 to 1843), a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in 1844, and a diagnosis of epilepsy in 1849, shortly before he was taken to the prison at Omsk; another says the first symptoms appeared in early adulthood and the diagnosis came about a decade later; a third calls the onset controversial. [R]
He was sentenced to four years of forced labor at the Siberian prison in Omsk; his seizures worsened during his imprisonment, and by 1853 he was quite debilitated by epilepsy. [D]
He described lack of sleep, alcohol, and overwork as triggers of his seizures, and he felt that the illness had damaged his memory. [D]

The type of his epilepsy is disputed: it has been interpreted as temporolimbic epilepsy, as an idiopathic generalized epilepsy with minor temporal involvement, as a cryptogenic focal epilepsy of frontomedial or temporal origin, and, for the ecstatic onset he described, as insular in origin. [R]
Whether the ecstatic experience he described before some seizures, and gave to characters in his fiction, was an epileptic aura is disputed. [R]
He portrayed up to six characters with epilepsy in his fiction, from Murin in The Landlady (1847) to Smerdyakov in The Brothers Karamazov (1880). [D]

His passion for roulette began on a tour of Europe in 1863. He fell into a pattern of chasing his losses and often pawned belongings so that he could gamble further. He gambled at Wiesbaden, Baden-Baden, and Bad Homburg, and the compulsion caused repeated financial trouble for about ten years. [D]
After returning to Russia he wrote the novella The Gambler, set in a fictional spa town called Roulettenburg, in 26 days. [D]
One retrospective review links his gambling to his epilepsy: the stress of gambling, together with sleep deprivation, is described as aggravating his seizures. [R]

text.paragraph: No medications started by this date.

Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, articulate, and intense; thought process organized; insight into the harm from gambling; no psychosis. Mood worried; PHQ-9 8 and GAD-7 7; no thoughts of suicide or self-harm. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Independent in all activities of daily living; after a seizure he is confused and exhausted for several hours and has trouble remembering for a day or two. [S]

Vital signs recorded on 1865-02-03; see the Vital Signs section. Mental status: Alert, articulate, and intense; thought process organized; insight into the harm from gambling; no psychosis; Mood worried; PHQ-9 8 and GAD-7 7; no thoughts of suicide or self-harm. The physical examination is limited to the findings relevant to this synthetic episode. [S]

Structured safety assessment: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent, access to means reviewed: yes. Routine outpatient care. Gambling disorder carries a raised suicide risk, especially after large losses, so safety is reviewed at every visit. He saved the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and the National Problem Gambling Helpline in his phone and agreed to call either after a large loss or if hopeless thoughts appear. Antiseizure medicine is dispensed as a 30-day supply. [S]

list.item: Epilepsy of unknown type with recurrent generalized tonic-clonic seizures of unknown onset, untreated for many years; etiology unknown: active, confirmed [S]
Gambling disorder (roulette, in person and online), moderate, with debts: active, confirmed [S]

Neurology consultation for seizure classification, EEG and MRI review, and the choice of antiseizure medicine. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015); Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: Position Paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology (2017); ILAE classification of the epilepsies: Position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology (2017) [S]

Seizure safety at every visit: triggers (sleep loss, alcohol, overwork), showers rather than baths, no swimming or heights alone, no driving until seizure-free and cleared by his neurologist, a written seizure action plan for friends, and a SUDEP discussion. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults: Report of the Guideline Development Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology and the American Epilepsy Society (2015); Practice guideline summary: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy incidence rates and risk factors (2017) [S]

Gambling-disorder treatment: cognitive behavioral therapy with a gambling-disorder therapist, self-exclusion, a bank gambling block, Gamblers Anonymous, and free debt counseling. Guideline: Psychological therapies for pathological and problem gambling (2012); Gambling disorder (2019) [S]

Mood and safety: PHQ-9 at intake and every two to four months, GAD-7 at intake and with any change, and a suicide-risk review with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at every visit. Guideline: ILAE clinical practice recommendations for the medical treatment of depression in adults with epilepsy (2022); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]
